p1(1−p1) = 0.0044 × 0.9956 = 0.00438064
p2(1−p2) = 0.0074 × 0.9926 = 0.00734524
Sum = 0.01172588

**6. Z-term.**
(1.96 + 0.8416)² = (2.8016)² = 7.84896

**7. Numerator.**
7.84896 × 0.01172588 = 0.0920359

**8. Denominator.**
(p1 − p2)² = (0.003)² = 0.000009

**9. Divide.**
n = 0.0920359 / 0.000009 ≈ 10,226 sessions per arm

**10. Check against the observed rates instead of the rounded 0.3-point figure.** Using the actual observed rates (0.44% and 0.75%, a 0.31-point difference, p2 = 0.0075) instead of the rounded MDE: p1(1−p1) = 0.00438064, p2(1−p2) = 0.0075 × 0.9925 = 0.00744375, sum = 0.01182439. Numerator = 7.84896 × 0.01182439 = 0.0928091. Denominator = (0.0031)² = 0.00000961. n = 0.0928091 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,661 sessions per arm.

**11. Discrepancy.** Both versions of this calculation land at roughly 9,700–10,200 sessions per arm, using this experiment's own control rate and the stated effect size, with the standard two-proportion formula at α = 0.05 and 80% power. 1. The query has two predicates: `date_trunc('day', created_at) = $1` and `tenant_id = $2`. Only `tenant_id` has an index (`events_tenant_id_idx`, single-column btree). `date_trunc(created_at)` has no index at all, so no access path can use it to narrow rows — it can only be applied as a row-by-row filter after the rows are fetched, whichever path is chosen.

2. That leaves the planner two real options for getting candidate rows: an index scan on `events_tenant_id_idx` (find the TIDs for `tenant_id = $2`, then fetch each row from the heap and filter by `date_trunc`), or a sequential scan of the whole table (read every row and filter by both conditions).

3. The planner picks between these by estimated cost, and the cost of the index path depends on how many rows `tenant_id = $2` matches — that comes from table statistics (the most-common-values / histogram stats Postgres keeps on `tenant_id`).

4. For the tenant the dashboard queries, that's about 38% of the table — roughly 15.6M of 41.2M rows.

5. A btree index on `tenant_id` only stores `tenant_id` and a heap pointer, not the other columns the query needs (`created_at`, `event_type`, `amount_cents`). So for every matching row, the executor has to do a separate heap fetch to get the actual row. At 38% of the table, that's on the order of 15.6M heap fetches.

6. Those heap fetches are not sequential — the matching rows are scattered across the table in whatever physical order they were inserted, not sorted by `tenant_id`. So the index path cost is dominated by random I/O: one random page access per matching row (Postgres's cost model charges a higher per-page cost for random access than for sequential access, by default about 4x).

7. A sequential scan, by contrast, reads every page of the table exactly once, in physical order — all sequential I/O, at the lower per-page cost, even though it touches all 41.2M rows instead of 15.6M.

8. Past a certain fraction of the table matching the indexed predicate, the random-access cost of an index path exceeds the cost of one full sequential pass, even with 2.5x fewer rows touched. That crossover typically lands well under 38% for a non-clustered index, so at 38% selectivity the sequential scan comes out cheaper in the planner's cost estimate.

9. Even a bitmap index scan — which sorts the TIDs first to turn scattered fetches into fewer, more sequential heap-page reads — doesn't rescue this: at 38% of the table, the bitmap ends up covering most of the table's pages anyway, so it degrades toward touching nearly as many pages as a sequential scan while adding the extra index-read overhead on top.

10. The index also doesn't help narrow toward the final answer, since the actual selective predicate is the date filter, which isn't indexed. Using the tenant index only gets you to 15.6M candidate rows; the date filter still has to be applied row-by-row afterward to bring that down to 612. So the index buys reduced row count but not reduced cost, once random I/O is accounted for.

11. That's why the plan shows a plain `Seq Scan on events` with `Filter: (tenant_id = $2 AND date_trunc(...) = $1)` — the planner computed both paths' cost and the sequential scan won, for this tenant's selectivity.

12. FINDINGS.md notes this flips for a small tenant: if `tenant_id = $2` matched a small fraction of the table, the number of random heap fetches would be small enough that the index path would beat a full sequential scan, and the planner would choose it. The dashboard happens to always query the largest tenant, so it always lands on the losing side of that comparison.

Standard formula for this: two-proportion z-test, two-sided test, α = 0.05, power = 80%.

**Step 1 — fix the test parameters.**
Two-sided test at α = 0.05 gives z_(α/2) = 1.960. Power of 80% means β = 0.20, giving z_β = 0.842.

**Step 2 — state the inputs.**
Control rate p1 = 0.0044, treatment rate p2 = 0.0075, so the effect to detect is Δ = p2 − p1 = 0.0031 (the 0.3-point figure the document rounds to).

**Step 3 — compute the variance term.**
The standard (Fleiss) formula uses the sum of each arm's own variance:
p1(1−p1) = 0.0044 × 0.9956 = 0.0043806
p2(1−p2) = 0.0075 × 0.9925 = 0.0074438
Sum = 0.0118244

**Step 4 — combine the z-values.**
(z_(α/2) + z_β) = 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802
Squared: 2.802² = 7.849

**Step 5 — assemble the formula.**
n per arm = (z_(α/2) + z_β)² × [p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2)] / Δ²
n = 7.849 × 0.0118244 / 0.0031²
n = 0.092808 / 0.00000961
n ≈ 9,658 sessions per arm

That is the standard derivation, and it lands at roughly 9,700 per arm, not 34,000. I ran it again three ways to check — pooled variance using the average rate p̄ = 0.00595 (≈9,660), using only the control rate as the baseline variance (≈7,150), and with the Fleiss continuity correction added on top of the first version (≈10,300) — and none land near 34,000. To reach ~34,000 with this Δ, the power would have to be pushed to roughly 99.9% rather than 80%, or the variance term inflated by close to 4x through some assumption not stated anywhere in the document.

So: I can't reconstruct a standard 80%-power, α = 0.05 derivation that produces 34,000 from these two rates. The document states that number without showing its work, and the number I get from the calculation it describes is about a third of that.

Neither `created_at` nor the `date_trunc` expression has an index, so `events_tenant_id_idx` is the only index that could possibly help either predicate.

2. `date_trunc('day', created_at)` is an expression, and there's no index on that expression, so this predicate can never be evaluated by an index lookup — no matter which access path the planner picks for the table, this predicate is always applied afterward, as a `Filter`, against whatever rows the access path produces. This means the date_trunc predicate plays no role in the choice between seq scan and index scan; that choice turns entirely on the `tenant_id` predicate.

3. So the planner's real decision is: to find rows where `tenant_id = $2`, scan the whole table sequentially and filter, or use `events_tenant_id_idx` to jump straight to matching rows.

4. The planner estimates the selectivity of `tenant_id = $2` from table statistics (`pg_stats`, specifically the most-common-values list and its frequencies for `tenant_id`). For the largest tenant, that stored frequency is 38% of the table, so the planner expects the index to identify roughly 0.38 × 41.2M ≈ 15.7 million matching rows.

5. An index scan isn't self-sufficient here: the index only stores `tenant_id` and the heap tuple pointer, not `created_at` or `amount_cents`, so for every matching index entry the planner must also fetch the corresponding heap page to get the other columns and apply the `date_trunc` filter. That's one heap access per matching row.

6. Those heap accesses, reached via an index scan, are costed as random I/O (`random_page_cost`, default 4) rather than sequential I/O (`seq_page_cost`, default 1), because index entries for a given tenant aren't guaranteed to be physically clustered together on disk — the planner checks the `correlation` statistic on `tenant_id` for this, and absent strong correlation, it assumes scattered access.

7. At 38% match rate, with rows scattered roughly uniformly across the table, the set of matching rows is expected to touch nearly every heap page at least once anyway — so an index scan wouldn't even reduce the number of pages read relative to a seq scan, it would just pay the random-access price for touching about the same pages a seq scan would read sequentially for free.

8. A seq scan, by contrast, reads every page once, in physical order, at the cheaper sequential rate, and evaluates both predicates (`tenant_id = $2` and the `date_trunc` filter) in one pass per row.

9. Comparing the two cost estimates, the seq scan comes out cheaper — this matches the actual plan, which shows `Seq Scan on events (cost=0.00..8817278.00 ...)` chosen over any index path, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` confirms the row counts (41,199,388 removed by filter, 612 kept) are consistent with that estimate.

10. This crossover — where scanning a large-enough fraction of a table via an index stops paying off versus reading it all sequentially — is a standard cost-based tradeoff, not specific to this query; a smaller tenant (a few percent of the table) would flip the estimate and make the index scan cheaper, which is consistent with the finding that `events_tenant_id_idx` would help for small tenants but not for the one the dashboard queries.

The core problem the file itself diagnoses: with only 11 total purchases (4 vs. 7), the reported **+70% lift** is a ratio estimator dividing by a tiny count — moving one purchase swings it from +36% to +125%, so it's noise dressed up as a finding, not an interval-estimation gap.

It also flags that the "obvious fix" doesn't work either: switching to the absolute difference (+0.31pp) is better-behaved but the study is wildly underpowered to detect it — this sample (912/934) needs ~34,000 sessions per arm at 80% power for a 0.3pp effect. So no metric on this data supports a ship decision.

Everything else (balance checks, ad-blocker loss, instrumentation, time-to-purchase) is noted as non-decisive — the time-to-purchase delta is called out as suffering the same small-sample problem (measured on 11 purchases).

Confidence: moderate on assignment, moderate-to-low on instrumentation, and in both cases the confidence is bounded by what the document actually verifies rather than what it asserts.

**Assignment**

The document reports balance on two covariates: device mix (61% vs 59% mobile) and returning-visitor share (23% vs 22%). Both gaps are small and directionally what you'd want from a working randomizer. But neither gap is accompanied by a test statistic or interval, so "balanced" is a visual judgment, not a demonstrated one — at roughly 900 sessions per arm, a 2-point gap in a binary covariate is plausible under pure chance, but so would be a somewhat larger one, and the document doesn't say where the line was drawn. This matters more than it would in a normal-sized experiment: the same small-N fragility that makes the purchase-rate lift unstable (a single purchase swinging it from +36% to +125%) also applies to any covariate check run on this sample. Two balanced covariates is reassuring but is not evidence that assignment was balanced on covariates that weren't checked.

The document doesn't state whether assignment was on session id in a way that could put the same user in both arms across separate sessions (browser-side vs. account-side identity), only that assignment was "on session id." If the checkout flow allows a user to abandon and return, session-level assignment with no user-level consistency guarantee would let a single user contribute to both counts. The document neither raises nor rules this out, so it's an open question rather than a settled one.

Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter, and the document notes this was deliberate and recorded in the experiment plan — that's the one assignment fact here that's fully accounted for, since it's a documented design choice rather than an observed property being asserted as fine.

**Instrumentation**

The document states the instrumentation "fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream," with no description of how that was checked (log completeness audit, event-count reconciliation against server-side records, etc.). Taken as given, it's a clean claim; taken as a claim to evaluate, it's asserted rather than shown.

The ad-blocker loss (0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event, evenly across arms) is the one instrumentation fact given a number, and the number is reassuring on its face. But "same rate in both arms" establishes that the volume of loss is symmetric, not that the composition of who is lost is symmetric. If ad-blocker users differ systematically from non-users in purchase propensity, and 0.3% of each arm's population is silently dropped or misclassified, that's a source of differential composition even at equal rates — the document asserts "does not bias the comparison" as a conclusion without showing the composition check that would support it. On a base of 4 and 7 purchases, this is exactly the kind of contamination that has outsized leverage relative to a larger experiment, because it takes very few affected sessions to move the numerator.

**Net assessment**: nothing in the document points to assignment or instrumentation being broken, and the checks that are present (device mix, visitor share, symmetric ad-blocker loss, deliberate logged-out exclusion) are all consistent with a clean run. The gap is that "consistent with clean" here rests on two covariate checks without significance framing, an unstated identity model for repeat sessions, and an instrumentation-integrity claim with no described method — and given how few purchases the whole readout rests on, unverified assumptions in this section carry more weight than they would in a well-powered experiment.

**Setup**

The claim is a standard two-proportion sample-size calculation: how many sessions per arm are needed to detect the difference between a control rate and a treatment rate, at a given significance level and power.

Inputs taken directly from the document:
- p₁ (control rate) = 0.44% = 0.0044
- p₂ (treatment rate) = 0.75% = 0.0075
- Δ = p₂ − p₁ = 0.0031 (the 0.31 percentage points reported earlier)
- Power = 80% (1 − β = 0.80), as stated in the document
- Significance level: not stated in the document, so the standard default is used — α = 0.05, two-sided

**Step 1 — Look up the z-values**

- z_{α/2} for α = 0.05 two-sided: z_{0.025} = 1.96
- z_β for 80% power: z_{0.20} = 0.8416

**Step 2 — Compute each arm's variance term**

- p₁(1−p₁) = 0.0044 × 0.9956 = 0.00438064
- p₂(1−p₂) = 0.0075 × 0.9925 = 0.00744375
- Sum = 0.01182439

**Step 3 — Compute the pooled variance term (used for the z_{α/2} part of the formula)**

- p̄ = (p₁+p₂)/2 = 0.00595, q̄ = 1 − p̄ = 0.99405
- 2p̄q̄ = 2 × 0.00595 × 0.99405 = 0.0118328

**Step 4 — Combine into the standard formula**

n (per arm) = [z_{α/2}·√(2p̄q̄) + z_β·√(p₁q₁+p₂q₂)]² / Δ²

- √(2p̄q̄) = √0.0118328 = 0.10878
- √(p₁q₁+p₂q₂) = √0.01182439 = 0.10874
- 1.96 × 0.10878 = 0.21321
- 0.8416 × 0.10874 = 0.09151
- Sum = 0.30472
- Squared = 0.09285

**Step 5 — Divide by Δ²**

- Δ² = 0.0031² = 0.00000961
- n = 0.09285 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,662, rounded up to whole sessions per arm ≈ 9,700

**Discrepancy**

Working the document's own stated inputs (0.44%, 0.75%, 80% power) through the standard two-proportion sample-size formula with the conventional default of α = 0.05 two-sided gives roughly 9,700 sessions per arm, not 34,000 — about a third of the document's figure. I checked this against a second, simplified version of the same formula (n ≈ 16·p̄q̄/Δ²) and got ≈9,850, consistent with the derivation above, so this isn't an arithmetic slip on one formula variant.

To land at ~34,000 from these same inputs requires materially stricter assumptions than "80% power" alone states — for example, α ≈ 0.01 paired with ~99% power gets to ≈29,600, and 99.9% power at α = 0.01 overshoots to ≈39,500. Neither of those is what "80% power" conventionally implies. I can't tell from the document which assumption (a stricter significance level, higher power, a multiple-comparisons correction, or a smaller target effect than the observed 0.31pp) produced 34,000, but under the plain reading of the document's own stated parameters, that figure doesn't reproduce.

   Attempt `CREATE INDEX events_day_idx ON events (date_trunc('day', created_at));` (no timezone argument) on a non-production copy or with `EXPLAIN` only. Confirms: Postgres raises `functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE`, validating that the timezone argument is required.

8. **Confirm the timezone-qualified expression index does what's claimed.**
   On a test/staging copy: `CREATE INDEX events_day_tenant_idx ON events (date_trunc('day', created_at, 'UTC'), tenant_id);` then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the query rewritten to use `date_trunc('day', created_at, 'UTC') = $1`. Confirms: plan switches from `Seq Scan` to an index-based scan (`Index Scan` or `Bitmap Index Scan`) and execution time drops from ~9s to milliseconds.

9. **Confirm the session/server timezone matches the assumption.**
   `SHOW timezone;` and check what `$1` is set to by the application (UTC day boundary or local-zone day boundary). Confirms: whichever fix is chosen produces the same day buckets the application currently relies on — a mismatch here would silently change which rows match.

10. **Sanity-check the ruled-out causes are still true at check time**, since FINDINGS.md's numbers are a point-in-time snapshot:
    - Pool usage: check current pool metrics, confirm still well under the 20 max.
    - Bloat: `SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events';`, confirm dead-tuple ratio is still low single digits.
    - Poll overlap: confirm query duration is still well under the 30s poll interval, so no queueing.

The argument, step by step:

1. **Two predicates, one indexable.** The `WHERE` clause has `tenant_id = $2` (matches `events_tenant_id_idx`) and `date_trunc('day', created_at) = $1` (matches no index — nothing on the table indexes that expression). Any plan the optimizer considers can use an index for the tenant condition at best; the date condition can only ever be evaluated as a row-by-row filter after a row is already fetched.

2. **What using the tenant index would actually cost.** If the planner picks `events_tenant_id_idx`, the shape of that plan is: walk the btree for `tenant_id = $2`, get a set of row locations (TIDs), then fetch each one from the heap and apply the `date_trunc` condition as a filter on top. The date condition cannot narrow the walk itself — it only discards rows after they've already been paid for.

3. **How many rows that walk touches.** The largest tenant, which is the one the dashboard queries, is 38% of the table — about 15.6 million of the 41.2 million rows. So the index path isn't a cheap lookup of a handful of rows; it's a scan of over a third of the table's rows via the index, each one requiring a separate heap fetch.

4. **Why those heap fetches are expensive.** Rows are inserted in time order, not tenant order, so a given tenant's rows are scattered essentially uniformly across the table's pages rather than clustered together. An index scan that returns 15.6 million scattered row locations turns into close to 15.6 million separate random-access page reads against the heap.

5. **Random I/O versus sequential I/O in the cost model.** Postgres's planner charges a per-page cost for each access method: `seq_page_cost` (default 1) for pages read sequentially, `random_page_cost` (default 4) for pages read via an index-driven fetch. A sequential scan reads all of the table's pages once, in order, at the cheap rate. The index path here reads a large fraction of the table's rows at the expensive, random rate — and still has to read close to that many distinct pages, since 15.6 million rows spread over a 41-million-row table touch most of the table's pages anyway.

6. **The comparison the planner actually makes.** Seq scan cost ≈ all pages × `seq_page_cost`. Index-then-heap-fetch cost ≈ (btree traversal cost) + 15.6 million × `random_page_cost`-weighted heap fetches. Because the tenant is not a small slice of the table, the second number comes out higher than the first — the index path was supposed to save I/O by touching fewer rows, and at 38% selectivity it no longer does.

7. **The date predicate can't tip this back.** Even though only 612 rows survive both conditions, the planner has no index that reflects `date_trunc('day', created_at)`, so it has no way to shrink the 15.6 million candidate set before the heap fetches happen. The eventual selectivity of the full `WHERE` clause is irrelevant to this comparison — what matters is the cost of the cheapest path to material rows the filter can be applied to, and the tenant index doesn't reduce that below the seq scan's cost.

8. **What the chosen plan confirms.** The plan's top-level `Seq Scan` node applies both conditions together as one `Filter`, discarding 41,199,388 of 41,200,000 rows to keep 612 — meaning the planner settled the access-method decision on `tenant_id` selectivity alone (38%, not small enough to make the index path cheaper), then ran both predicates as post-scan filtering regardless of which path it picked. That's the whole reason the index exists on disk but never appears in the plan.

No. That's the ticket's original proposal, and FINDINGS.md says it can't serve this query: a plain btree on `created_at` is ordered by the raw timestamp, but the predicate compares `date_trunc('day', created_at)` to `$1`, so the planner can't match the two — the plan stays a seq scan.

The two fixes that do work: an expression index on `date_trunc('day', created_at, 'UTC')` plus `tenant_id`, or rewriting the predicate to a half-open range on `created_at` paired with a `(tenant_id, created_at)` composite index.

turns.text:
The document already diagnoses its own problem, correctly: the reported **+70% lift** is a ratio built on 4 vs. 7 purchases, so noise this small (one purchase moving either way) swings the headline from +36% to +125% — a number with no stable interval, not evidence about the checkout flow. It also correctly rejects the fallback of reporting the +0.31pp absolute difference as a fix, since resolving a 0.3-point gap at these conversion rates needs ~34,000 sessions/arm against an actual 912/934 — nowhere close to powered.

The one weak spot is the closing aside on median time-to-purchase (4m12s → 3m01s): it's flagged as "real" while resting on the same 11-purchase sample the rest of the document says can't resolve anything, so calling it "real" is inconsistent with the document's own standard.

Low-to-moderate confidence. The document asserts these points without showing the evidence behind them, and the sample is small enough that the checks themselves are underpowered for what they're being used to establish.

**Assignment balance.** The balance check covers two covariates — device mix and returning-visitor share — and reports them as point percentages (61%/59%, 23%/22%) with no test or interval attached. On ~1,846 total sessions, two-point gaps like these are consistent with clean randomization, but they're also consistent with mild imbalance that a formal test would flag; "looks balanced" here is an eyeball judgment, not a demonstrated one. More importantly, checking two covariates says nothing about others (traffic source, campaign, time-of-day mix) that could differ between arms and correlate with purchase propensity. With only 11 purchases total, it would not take much covariate imbalance to produce the 4-vs-7 split on its own, and nothing in the document rules that out.

**Ad-blocker loss.** The claim that both arms lose 0.3% of sessions to ad-blocker interference "at the same rate" is stated with no per-arm counts given, so there's no way to check it from the document itself. Even if the rate is truly equal, sessions lost to an ad blocker are not a random subsample of all sessions — ad-blocker users skew toward particular browsers and behaviors — so their exclusion could still shift the composition of each arm's remaining sessions in ways that don't show up as a rate difference.

**Logged-out exclusion.** The document notes this filter was deliberate and documented in the experiment plan, which addresses whether the exclusion itself was intentional, but not whether it behaves identically across arms. A single-page and a two-page checkout can differ in when a session's login state becomes visible to the assignment filter; if that timing differs between the two flows, the same nominal rule could exclude a different mix of sessions per arm. The document doesn't check for this.

**Instrumentation.** "Fired correctly throughout, no gaps in the event stream" is the least supported claim in the document — there's no count, completeness ratio, or method given for how this was verified. It's also ambiguous which event stream is meant: the assignment event, or the full funnel through to the purchase event that the entire headline number depends on. Given that the whole analysis hinges on 11 purchase events being counted correctly, this is the claim I'd want the most evidence behind, and it currently has none.

**General point.** All four of these checks are being used to certify that the arms are comparable, but with 11 purchases total, none of them have the statistical power to detect the size of assignment or instrumentation problem that would actually explain a 4-vs-7 split. The document labels them "none decisive" for the lift number, which is correct, but the same smallness that makes the lift number unusable also makes these supporting checks weak evidence of a clean experiment, not just weak evidence of an effect.

The standard formula for required sample size per arm to detect a difference between two proportions, at significance level α and power (1−β), with equal-sized arms:

n = [z_(α/2)·√(2·p̄·(1−p̄)) + z_β·√(p1·(1−p1) + p2·(1−p2))]² / (p1−p2)²

Step 1 — inputs from the table. Control rate p1 = 0.44% = 0.0044, treatment rate p2 = 0.75% = 0.0075 (these are the document's own rounded figures; the raw rates are 4/912 = 0.4386% and 7/934 = 0.7495%, close enough not to matter here). The absolute difference is p2 − p1 = 0.0031, which the document rounds to "0.3 points."

Step 2 — critical values. Two-sided test at α = 0.05 gives z_(α/2) = 1.95996. 80% power gives z_β = 0.84162. These are the conventional defaults and the document doesn't state otherwise, so I've used them.

Step 3 — pooled proportion for the α term. p̄ = (p1+p2)/2 = 0.00595, q̄ = 1−p̄ = 0.99405.

Step 4 — the two variance terms inside the brackets.
z_(α/2)·√(2·p̄·q̄) = 1.95996 × √(2 × 0.00595 × 0.99405) = 1.95996 × 0.10877 = 0.21317
z_β·√(p1(1−p1)+p2(1−p2)) = 0.84162 × √(0.0044×0.9956 + 0.0075×0.9925) = 0.84162 × √(0.011824) = 0.84162 × 0.10874 = 0.09152

Step 5 — sum and square. (0.21317 + 0.09152)² = 0.30469² = 0.092848

Step 6 — divide by delta². 0.0031² = 0.00000961. n = 0.092848 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,660 per arm.

That's the full standard calculation, and it lands at roughly 9,700 sessions per arm, not 34,000 — even rounding delta to exactly 0.003 (0.3 points flat, discarding the extra 0.01) only brings it up to about 10,300. Both are a factor of roughly 3.3–3.5 below the document's stated figure. I can't reproduce 34,000 from these rates using the standard two-proportion sample-size formula under any of the ordinary parameter choices (95% two-sided / 80% power, or 90%/80%, or using either rounded or exact rates) — the document's number doesn't check out against its own inputs, and I'm not able to reconstruct what calculation would produce it.

turns.text:
Two compounding causes:

1. **Trigger**: release `v412` changed config `PAYMENTS_SETTLEMENT_MODE` from `legacy` to `split`. Instances still running `v411` code didn't recognize `split`, so `assertSettlementMode()` threw on any unrecognized value, producing 500s on `POST /checkout`.
2. **What made it unrecoverable**: migration `0042` (triggered by the same `v412` release job) added a `NOT NULL` column `settlement_currency` to `ledger_entries` with no default. Once that ran, `v411`'s `chargeOrder()` — which never writes that column — could no longer insert successfully. So reverting the config back to `legacy`, and later rolling back to `v411`, both failed: they restored the old insert path against a schema that now rejected it. The error changed (from mode assertion to not-null violation) but the error rate didn't drop.

Fixed by `v413`, which kept `split` mode/the new column but dropped the `NOT NULL` constraint, backfilled existing rows, then re-applied `NOT NULL`.

The document only reports impact as checkout error rate over time, not customer or revenue counts. Phase by phase:

- **13:58–14:02** — `v412` rolling out, one instance at a time. No customer impact yet.
- **14:02** — First 500s on `POST /checkout`. Error rate goes from 0% to 34% in ninety seconds. Every checkout attempt hitting an instance on the bad config/version combination fails.
- **14:02–14:05** — Errors continue at the 14:02 level; the rollout is still placing more instances on `v412`.
- **14:05** — Migration `0042_add_settlement_currency` runs. No visible change in error rate at this moment, but this is the point past which the outage cannot be undone by reverting config or code, since the new `NOT NULL` column now rejects the old insert path.
- **14:09** — Team paged. Error rate at 61%, three of four instances now on `v412`. Impact roughly triples from the 14:02 reading.
- **14:09–14:14** — Error rate holds near 61% while on-call investigates.
- **14:14** — Root cause misdiagnosed as the `PAYMENTS_SETTLEMENT_MODE` config flip (correct partial diagnosis, but incomplete).
- **14:21** — Config reverted to `legacy`. Error rate does not recover — holds at 58%. Checkout remains broken for customers; the failure mode changes from a mode assertion to a not-null violation, invisible to users.
- **14:21–14:33** — Error rate remains at 58% for twelve minutes while the team reassesses.
- **14:33** — Attempt to roll back the release to `v411`. New instances coming up on `v411` also fail (same not-null violation). No recovery.
- **14:33–14:41** — Error rate remains elevated (no figure given for this stretch beyond the 58% baseline) while the actual root cause — migration plus config, not config alone — is worked out.
- **14:41** — Root cause fully understood; forward fix written.
- **14:41–14:47** — Error rate presumably still elevated while `v413` is built and deployed (no figure given).
- **14:47** — `v413` deployed. Error rate returns to 0% within two minutes.

Total window: 14:02–14:47 (45 minutes), consistent with the report's header of 14:02–14:47 and severity classified as Sev1. Checkout was substantially degraded (34%–61% error rates) for the full 45 minutes, with two failed recovery attempts (config revert at 14:21, release rollback at 14:33) that did not reduce the error rate.

No `chargeOrder()` source in this directory — only `INCIDENT.md` exists here. That file describes the behavior, not the code:

- Under `split`, `chargeOrder()` writes two ledger rows per order instead of one (vs. one row under `legacy`).
- Each of those rows must carry a `settlement_currency` value.

That's the full extent of what INCIDENT.md states about the `split`-mode change — it doesn't show the function body or any other diffs.

| What went well | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Fast initial detection/page | Error rate hit 34% at 14:02; paged by 14:09 — seven minutes. |
| Correctly identified the config change | On-call found `PAYMENTS_SETTLEMENT_MODE` had flipped to `split` at 14:14, five minutes after paging. |
| Ruled out plausible red herrings efficiently | Report lists DB CPU/connections, payment provider, the `pg_stat_activity` spike, and load as checked and excluded, so investigation didn't stall chasing them. |
| Forward fix resolved the outage fast once root cause was found | `v413` deployed at 14:47, error rate to 0% within two minutes. |
| Post-incident write-up is thorough | Timeline, root cause, and three concrete action items produced same day. |

| What did not go well | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Diagnosis stopped at the config change, missed the migration | 14:14 identified only the config flip; the migration's role wasn't understood until 14:41 — 27 minutes later. |
| First recovery attempt (config revert) didn't work and cost time | Reverted at 14:21; error rate held at 58%, no recovery. |
| Second recovery attempt (release rollback) also didn't work | Attempted at 14:33; instances on `v411` also 500'd — twelve minutes after the failed config revert, before this was tried. |
| Migration ran inside the rollback window | `0042` executed at 14:05, triggered automatically by the `v412` release job, three minutes into the outage — made both later recovery attempts fail. Named directly as action item 2. |
| Migration shipped unsafe for rollback | `NOT NULL` column with no default, added in the same release as the code that first populates it — a violation of expand/contract, named as action item 1. |
| Unknown-mode handling was a hard failure | `assertSettlementMode()` threw on any unrecognized value rather than degrading — named as action item 3. |
| Total resolution time | 45 minutes (14:02–14:47) start to full recovery, with two failed intermediate attempts. |

No — the trigger, not the cause. The config change (`legacy`→`split`) started the errors at 14:02.
